name: Ben Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast hole drill at Kestrel Range, an open-pit iron ore mine. The drill is a big tracked rig that bores holes about fifteen metres deep in a pattern, and the blast crew fills them with explosive. I follow a drill plan on a screen in the cab, line up each hole with GPS, and log how hard the rock was so the engineers can plan the blast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the tech side. The rig has GPS, sensors, all sorts, and I'm always asking the engineers questions. What wears me out is the noise and the money. I share a house with two other guys from the mine, and I put most of my savings into a laptop and an online course in automation last year, so right now I've got about three weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what a waste. All that talk, and the best we got was a better spellchecker. I'd still be telling people the robots in mining are real even if the chatbots were hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a bit of a let-down for me. I bet on the tech side with that course, and if nothing radical changes, that bet pays slower. The drill rig I run already has an autonomous mode that nobody switches on, and I'd be the one asking why not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep doing the automation course at night, because mines will still buy more automation even if chat AI flops. I'd use AI every day like I already do, for study notes and planning my week. And I'd try to get back to a month of savings by Christmas, since I spent it all on the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit impatient. My job's safe, but it's the same job for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does nobody switch the autonomous mode on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The supervisors say it's slower than a good operator and nobody's been trained on it. I think they're also nervous the union will kick up, and honestly, as a union member, I get that. I just think we should be the ones running it, not waiting for it to run us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You put your savings into a course. Any second thoughts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, when the car needed tyres and I had to put them on a card. But I'd do it again. Thin savings worry me, but being stuck worries me more.

say: I'd say the chat AI was **hype**, but robots in mining are still real.
I'd tell people we got a **better spellchecker** and little else.
think: My **automation course** pays off slower if nothing radical changes.
The rig's unused **autonomous mode** shows where mining is heading anyway.
do: Keep **drilling** at Kestrel Range on the same roster.
Rebuild **a month of savings** by Christmas.
feel: Mostly fine, a bit **impatient** at being stuck in one job.
S0.quote: The drill rig I run already has an autonomous mode that nobody switches on, and I'd be the one asking why not.
fieldNote: Ben is **disappointed** by a plateau because he bet his savings on automation.
He wants miners to **run the robots**, not wait to be replaced.
His thin cushion bothers him less than **being stuck**.

steps.text: Keep drilling blast hole patterns at Kestrel Range
Finish the online automation course at night
Rebuild a month of rent savings by Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for workers to get trained, paid, and put in charge of the new kit. I'd post about it, I'd raise it at the union, and I'd want government money for retraining, not just company goodwill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd see it as my chance. The office jobs feel it first, the planners and buyers, but the drill rigs will go autonomous eventually. I'd rather be the guy who sets up the robot drill than the guy who gets replaced by the robot drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd ask my supervisor to put me on the autonomous drill trial and train me on it. I'd apply for a job at the company's remote operations centre in the city, where they run rigs and trucks from screens. And I'd keep using AI tools daily to learn the control software faster than anyone else on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about that, because I know a lot of my mates won't feel the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, who's been on drills for twenty years and hates screens. He's better at reading rock than I'll ever be. I'd want the union to make sure guys like Rob get the same training I do, at their own pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to the city costs money. How would you manage that on three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to ask the company for relocation help, or crash on my cousin's floor for a couple of months. Rents in the city are brutal. I'd probably bring a mate from the mine and share a flat to make it work.

say: I'd say workers should be **trained** and put **in charge** of new kit.
I'd want **government money** for retraining, not company goodwill.
think: This picture is **my chance** to move into automation.
Drill rigs will go **autonomous** eventually, so I'd rather set them up.
do: Ask to join the **autonomous drill trial** in the first month.
Apply to the company's **remote operations centre** in the city.
Use AI tools daily to learn the **control software** fast.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with some **guilt** about mates who'll struggle.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the guy who sets up the robot drill than the guy who gets replaced by the robot drill.
fieldNote: Ben treats Steady Disruption as an **opening**, unlike most of his crew.
His progressive side shows in wanting **Rob**, a veteran driller, trained too.
The move to the city depends on **relocation help** he doesn't yet have.

steps.text: Ask the supervisor for a place on the autonomous drill trial
Apply for a job at the remote operations centre in the city
Use AI tools daily to learn the drill control software
Share a city flat with a mate from the mine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public money and fast rules, because companies won't share the gains on their own. I'd be backing the union and any politician who wants a tax on robots to fund people through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's scarier than I'd like to admit. With AGI in 2028, the remote operations centre in the city could be empty before I've finished paying for the course to work in it. The drilling itself lasts till about 2031, so I'd have three years of pay, but the job I was aiming at gets hit first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and save every dollar I could for the three years before the robots. I'd switch from the operations course to something the robots need people for, like field maintenance on autonomous rigs, sensors and wiring. And I'd join the union's working group on automation, because I'd know the tech better than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Usually I like change, but this one's moving faster than I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance, if robots are coming for hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first robots break a lot, and somebody has to climb up and fix them in the dust and heat. That's still hands-on, so it lasts till 2031 at least, maybe longer while the robots are new. It's not forever, but it buys me time to see what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. I'd sell it and get the mine bus, which saves me about four hundred a month. My housemates would laugh, but I'd have a cushion for once.

say: I'd say companies won't **share the gains** without public rules.
I'd back a **tax on robots** to fund people through the change.
think: The **remote operations** job I was aiming for gets hit first in 2028.
Drilling lasts until about **2031**, giving me three years of pay.
do: Switch study to **field maintenance** of autonomous rigs.
Sell the car and take the **mine bus** to save four hundred a month.
feel: **Unsettled**, because change is moving faster than he can.
S2.quote: With AGI in 2028, the remote operations centre in the city could be empty before I've finished paying for the course to work in it.
fieldNote: Ben sees AGI hit the **screen job** he planned before it hits his drill.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** to retrain into hands-on maintenance.
Selling the car shows he'll make **real cuts** despite his optimism.

steps.text: Switch study to maintaining sensors on autonomous drill rigs
Sell the car and ride the mine bus to save money
Join the union working group on automation
Vote for candidates who back a robot tax for retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if we start this year. I'd want the company, union and government in one room agreeing a training plan for every miner at Kestrel Range.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the one where I'd do best. Five years is long enough to learn the robots and short enough that I can't waste a single month of it. The thinking side goes by 2031 and robots around 2034, so I'd aim to be one of the people installing and fixing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the automation course, then get an electrical or instrumentation ticket over two years, part-time. I'd use AI to study, plan, everything. And I'd go for the autonomous drill trial and push the union to make it open to anyone who wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pumped, honestly. Nervous about money, but pumped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you pay for two years of part-time study on your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to fund it under the training agreement the union's pushing for. If they won't, I'd do it slowly and keep drilling full-time. It would be tight, but tight is normal for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2034, when robots can fix robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe nobody does. I'd hope that by then there's a proper public plan for people, because I can't out-learn a machine forever.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to do this properly if we start now.
I'd want company, union and government agreeing a **training plan** together.
think: This is the picture where I'd **do best** with time to learn.
I can't **out-learn** a machine forever after 2034.
do: Finish the **automation course**, then an instrumentation ticket over two years.
Join the **autonomous drill trial** and push for open access.
Ask the company to **fund the study**.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to learn the robots and short enough that I can't waste a single month of it.
fieldNote: Ben's adaptability shines when there's **enough time** to plan.
He openly says nobody knows what happens **after 2034**.
His long-term hope rests on a **public plan**, fitting his progressive views.

steps.text: Get an instrumentation ticket part-time over two years
Run the autonomous drill on the Kestrel Range trial
Use AI tools to study for the instrumentation ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to make sure nobody gets dumped. I'd be campaigning for free training for any miner who wants it, paid by a levy on the big mining companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd relax a little. Ten years means I can stop sprinting and pick a career, not just a lifeboat. By 2039 I'd be 40, and I'd have had time to get qualified, save a bit, maybe even buy a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling for two or three years while I finish my studies. Then I'd look at going to the city and doing an engineering technician diploma, something with planning and design. I'd keep using AI daily, and I'd try to save a month of pay each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. Still stretched for money, but the future looks like something I can shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said engineering technician, which is thinking work. Doesn't that get hit by AGI in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair point, it does, three years before the drill. So maybe I'd stay hands-on with the rigs and get the instrumentation ticket instead. I like ideas, but this picture says hands-on lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the decade go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting hurt, or the iron ore price crashing and Kestrel Range closing early. With three weeks of savings, a closure would hit me before any robot did.

I'd campaign for **free training** paid by a levy on mining companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be retraining for jobs that were disappearing while I studied, with no savings to fall back on. What would help is free training with a wage while you do it, so guys like me don't have to choose between rent and learning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who pays. Robots should pay for the retraining of the people they replace, the same way a mine pays to fix the land after it closes. That seems fair to me, and I don't hear anyone saying it.

headlineQuote: Robots should pay for the retraining of the people they replace, the same way a mine pays to fix the land after it closes.
portrait: Ben, 27, runs a **blast hole drill** at Kestrel Range iron ore mine and shares a house.
He spent his savings on an **automation course**, leaving about three weeks of rent.
He uses AI daily and treats change as a **chance**, not a threat.
He's uneasy in the slower pictures and **anxious** when AGI comes in two or five years.
He wants **robots taxed** to pay for retraining displaced miners.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be **retraining for jobs** that vanish while he studies.
whatWouldHelp: **Free training** with a wage, so miners don't choose between rent and learning.
